title: Jonathan Hall asks what happens when automated liquidity providers all step back together
summary: Jonathan Hall’s final speech as a member of the Financial Policy Committee starts with a distinction the Bank’s survey makes easy to miss. Eighty per cent of respondents to its survey with the Financial Conduct Authority used some form of agentic AI. Only 2% of the agents had broad autonomy, defined by the scope to initiate and execute actions with limited real-time human involvement. One denominator is survey respondents and the other is agents. Neither number measures the share of market liquidity supplied by autonomous systems. Hall is asking how delegation could change financial stability as that second measure grows.

He draws an analogy with his own institution. Parliament gives the Bank operational independence over how to pursue specified objectives, subject to limits on its instruments. It also expects published explanations and the ability to question decision-makers. Alignment with a mandate, constraints on action and accountability each do different work. Monitoring imposes costs on both parties. Hall argues that similar investments matter when financial firms give an automated agent discretion over real positions or funds. A record that a system generated a plausible explanation of an action cannot by itself establish why that action was chosen.

The market-wide question has three parts. Liquidity provision may become more concentrated among firms with the best technology. Independent firms’ actions may become more correlated on ordinary days. Firms that usually behave differently may also respond in the same way when losses or uncertainty rise. The chart using ten-year US Treasury futures illustrates concentration in passive trading by intermediaries over time. Its index describes the distribution of trading across providers. It neither identifies trades generated by modern AI agents nor measures how different providers would behave during a new shock. Concentration and correlation need separate tests.

Hall proposes comparing a population of rules-based portfolio managers with one of AI agents assigned similar styles. Measuring how closely the pairs match initially, whether they drift and how the populations respond to a change of regime could reveal behaviour obscured by average returns. He presents this as a research design. The diagrams contrasting specialised tools with more general agents describe possible organisations of investment decisions, without providing a performance comparison between them. Even firms that separate their strategies could ultimately depend on the same underlying model. In stress, its shared assumptions or a simultaneous decision by human managers to suspend activity could remove liquidity when it was most valuable.

Hall discusses both market-wide protections, including circuit breakers and limits on leverage, and controls within firms. One proposal would estimate the social cost of conduct already prohibited by market rules, allowing independent review or an internal check before an action proceeds. The difficulty lies in defining and validating the counterfactual effect on the market. He offers no calibrated threshold and announces no new regulation. His argument is that firms need credible ways of meeting existing obligations as they delegate more authority. For an investor relying on rapid order execution, evidence that several providers can stay in the market under the same stress would matter more than the number using AI in everyday operations.

questions.question: Would ostensibly independent liquidity providers withdraw at the same time?
questions.detail: Use venue-level data on providers, quoted depth, cancellations and completed transactions across calm and stressed intervals. Separate concentration in normal volume from correlation in the decision to reduce risk. Compare markets with different dependencies on model vendors or clearing arrangements. A high ordinary-day market share and a common withdrawal in stress imply different costs for an investor trying to exit a position.

questions.question: Do agents reproduce the intended mandates when the environment changes?
questions.detail: Hall proposes matching AI and rules-based managers by initial style. Compare their subsequent exposures, turnover, liquidity use and losses on identical data, including regimes withheld from design. Document model versions, mandate differences and intervention by human managers. A strategy may match its benchmark during calibration yet lose the diversification an owner expected during a funding or volatility shock.

questions.question: Can a compliance check distinguish prohibited conduct from legitimate liquidity provision?
questions.detail: Look for independent validation against exchange surveillance records, including false positives during volatile periods. Test how sensitive the estimated social cost is to the counterfactual market price and how quickly an accountable person can review a disputed decision. An excessively restrictive check could remove useful liquidity, while a permissive one leaves the delegating firm exposed to losses and regulatory action.
